b: Peter writes to believers scattered across what is now Turkey, mostly Gentiles, who were being slandered and mistreated for their faith. He tells them who they are: chosen, born again to a living hope, God’s own people, ‘foreigners and exiles’ whose real home is with God. Then he shows how to live in a hostile world: holy, submissive where possible, doing good, ready to explain their hope, and following Christ, who suffered unjustly without retaliating.
1 Peter is realistic about suffering without ever treating it as meaningless. It also contains one of the hardest passages in the New Testament, on Christ preaching ‘to the spirits in prison’ (3:19).

Where scholars stand. The letter claims to be from ‘Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ’ (1:1), who was ‘a witness of Christ’s sufferings’ (5:1). Many critical scholars think it was written later, perhaps AD 70–95, by a follower of Peter or a group in Rome, in his name. Their reasons: its good, rhythmic Greek and use of the Greek Old Testament seem beyond a Galilean fisherman (Acts 4:13); it sounds like Paul; it contains few personal memories of Jesus; and its picture of persecution may fit a later time.

The case for Peter. (1) The letter was used very early and always as Peter’s. Polycarp (early 2nd century) certainly used it, and Papias, of the same generation, ‘uses testimonies from the first Epistle of John and from that of Peter likewise’ (Eusebius). Irenaeus names Peter as author, and no early writer attributes it to anyone else. (2) The letter says it was written ‘Through Silvanus’ (5:12). Silvanus (Silas) was a Roman citizen, a leader of the Jerusalem church and Paul’s colleague. Ancient secretaries were often given real freedom in wording, which would explain both the polished Greek and the echoes of Paul. (3) Galilee was bilingual, and Peter’s own brother had a Greek name (Andrew). After thirty years of preaching across the Greek-speaking world, Peter is likely to have been at home in Greek. (4) The letter is full of echoes of Jesus’ sayings, especially from the Sermon on the Mount, used as remembered teaching rather than quotations. (5) A forger wanting authority would more naturally have used Paul’s name, since the letter is addressed partly to Paul’s mission field and shares his themes; and it contains no controversy that would need a borrowed name. (6) Nothing in its picture of persecution requires a date after the 60s (see below).

hist.t: ‘Babylon’, Mark, and Peter’s death in Rome
b: Peter sends greetings from ‘The church in Babylon’ (5:13). Babylon in Mesopotamia is unlikely (it would be a remarkable coincidence for Mark and Silvanus, Paul’s old colleagues, to be there too), and there was only a military post called Babylon in Egypt. Most scholars agree that ‘Babylon’ is a code-name for Rome, as in Revelation 14:8 and 17:5: the great, proud capital of a world opposed to God, where God’s people live as exiles.

Early Christian writers place Peter’s last years and death in Rome. Around AD 95, 1 Clement, written from Rome, says that ‘Peter, through unrighteous envy, endured not one or two, but numerous labours’ and ‘departed to the place of glory due to him’. Later tradition (reported by Eusebius from Origen) says he was crucified upside down, under Nero, probably in the mid 60s. ‘My son Mark’ (5:13) fits another early tradition, from Papias (early 2nd century): ‘Mark, having become the interpreter of Peter, wrote down accurately, though not in order, whatsoever he remembered of the things said or done by Christ.’

b: The readers were in five Roman provinces of what is now Turkey (1:1). They were suffering slander, insults and hostility from neighbours (2:12; 3:16; 4:4, 14), and a ‘fiery trial’ was coming (4:12). In AD 64, after the great fire of Rome, Nero blamed the Christians. The Roman historian Tacitus says they were named after ‘Christus’, who ‘had undergone the death penalty in the reign of Tiberius’ ‘by sentence of the procurator Pontius Pilatus’. Some ‘were covered with wild beasts’ skins and torn to death by dogs; or they were fastened on crosses’, and some were burned as torches. That persecution was in Rome, not in the provinces.

About AD 110, Pliny, governor of Bithynia-Pontus (two of the provinces named in 1:1), wrote to the emperor Trajan asking whether to punish Christians for ‘the name’ alone. Some scholars have dated 1 Peter to that time. But the New Bible Dictionary argues that 1 Peter’s language about ‘the name’ reflects the earliest Christian usage (compare Acts 5:41), and that the suffering it describes is mostly local hostility and injustice, not an official state campaign. Nothing requires a date later than the 60s.

1.t: Two words that set the tone. Chosen by God, and displaced in the world. Peter writes to people for whom the second is a daily experience.
Born again to an inheritance kept in heaven, guarded through faith. The grief of trials is acknowledged in the same breath as the joy — Peter does not choose between them.

2.t: Titles given to Israel at Sinai are applied to a mixed congregation of Jewish and Gentile believers. The stone imagery runs through Isaiah and Psalm 118.
Then immediately more than an example: he bore our sins in his body on the tree. Isaiah 53 supplies most of the vocabulary.

3.t: The verse apologetics takes its name from. Note the order: Christ set apart as Lord in the heart first, then readiness, then gentleness and respect. The manner is part of the instruction.

Christ preaching to spirits in prison is among the hardest passages in the New Testament, and the main readings are set out honestly in any good commentary. Nothing in Christian doctrine rests on settling it. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

4.t: Suffering for the name is presented as normal rather than exceptional. Peter's pastoral move is to remove the additional burden of feeling that something has gone wrong.

5.t: Peter writes to elders as a fellow elder, and tells them not to lord it over those entrusted to them. He of all people knew what he had been forgiven.
Grammatically, casting anxiety is how humbling yourself under God's hand is done. Worry is treated as a form of self-reliance.

1.ctx: Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia were Roman provinces covering much of modern Turkey.
1.mean: ‘Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, To the elect who are exiles of the Dispersion’. ‘Dispersion’ was the word for Jews living outside the land of Israel; Peter applies it to all believers, who are at home nowhere in this world. They are ‘chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father and sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling by His blood’. Father, Spirit and Son are named together in their work of salvation.
1.big: Believers are chosen by the Father, set apart by the Spirit and cleansed by the Son, and so are exiles in this world.
1.diff: ‘According to the foreknowledge of God’. Reformed: God’s foreknowledge here is his loving choice, not merely his seeing in advance who would believe. Calvin: ‘the foreknowledge of God excludes every worthiness on the part of man.’ Arminian: God chose those he foresaw would believe. Wesley, interestingly, pointed out that ‘Strictly speaking, there is no foreknowledge, no more than afterknowledge, with God’, since God sees all of time at once, and he described election here as God’s free love setting people apart. Both agree that salvation begins with God, not with us.

1.ctx: The letter opens, like many Jewish prayers, with a blessing of God.
1.mean: ‘By His great mercy He has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, and into an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you, who through faith are shielded by God’s power’. Trials come, but they prove faith genuine, ‘more precious than gold’. ‘Though you have not seen Him, you love Him’, and rejoice ‘with an inexpressible and glorious joy’. The prophets searched to understand this salvation; ‘Even angels long to look into these things.’
1.big: Believers have a living hope and an inheritance kept safe in heaven, and they are kept safe for it.
1.diff: ‘Shielded by God’s power’ ‘through faith’ (verse 5). Both God’s keeping and the believer’s faith are here. Reformed theology stresses that God keeps his people believing, so they will persevere (Westminster Confession 17). Arminian theology stresses that God keeps those who continue in faith. All agree the inheritance itself cannot fade.

1.ctx: ‘Prepare your minds for action’ is literally ‘gird up the loins of your mind’ (BSB footnote): tuck up the long robe ready to work or run.
1.mean: ‘Set your hope fully on the grace to be given you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.’ Do not live as before. ‘But just as He who called you is holy, so be holy in all you do, for it is written: “Be holy, because I am holy.”’ Live in reverent fear, because ‘it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed from the empty way of life you inherited from your forefathers, but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot.’
1.big: Those redeemed at such a cost are called to be holy like the God who called them.
1.diff: ‘The empty way of life you inherited from your forefathers’ suggests most readers were Gentiles who had grown up in pagan religion.

1.mean: ‘Love one another deeply, from a pure heart. For you have been born again, not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God.’ ‘All flesh is like grass… but the word of the Lord stands forever.’ ‘And this is the word that was proclaimed to you.’
1.big: New birth through God’s enduring word produces deep love among believers.

2.h: The Living Stone and Chosen People
2.ctx: Peter, whose name means ‘rock’, uses the image of stones. He draws together Isaiah 28:16, Psalm 118:22, Isaiah 8:14 and Exodus 19:6.
2.mean: ‘Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk’. Coming to Christ, ‘the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight, you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices’. ‘But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.’ Living ‘as foreigners and exiles’, they must live so well among unbelievers that slanderers ‘may see your good deeds and glorify God’.
2.big: Built on Christ, believers together are God’s temple and priesthood, called to show his goodness to the world.
2.diff: ‘A royal priesthood’. Peter gives the whole church titles once given to Israel at Sinai. At the Reformation this passage was central to the teaching of the priesthood of all believers: every Christian has direct access to God through Christ and offers ‘spiritual sacrifices’. Calvin: ‘ye are royal priests, and, indeed, in a more excellent way, because ye are, each of you, consecrated in Christ.’ Protestant churches do not have priests in a special sense; ministers are pastors and teachers. Catholic and Orthodox teaching affirm the ‘common priesthood’ of all the baptised, but hold that it differs from the ordained priesthood: ‘While being “ordered one to another,” they differ essentially’ (Catechism 1547).

2.ctx: ‘The king’ would mean the Roman emperor, possibly Nero.
2.mean: ‘Submit yourselves for the Lord’s sake to every human institution’, to the emperor and to governors ‘sent by him to punish those who do wrong and to praise those who do right.’ ‘Live in freedom, but do not use your freedom as a cover-up for evil; live as servants of God. Treat everyone with high regard: Love the brotherhood of believers, fear God, honor the king.’ Household slaves are to submit even to harsh masters: ‘if you suffer for doing good and you endure it, this is commendable before God.’
2.big: Christians honour earthly authorities and endure injustice patiently, as servants of God.
2.diff: Limits. Notice: ‘fear God, honor the king’. Only God is feared. When rulers command what God forbids, Peter himself said, ‘We must obey God rather than men’ (Acts 5:29). Christians differ on how far resistance to unjust rulers may go, but agree that submission to rulers is never absolute. Slavery. As with Paul, Peter addresses slaves as responsible believers in a world they could not change; this is not an endorsement of slavery.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Peter (trans. Owen), CCEL

2.ctx: Peter quotes and echoes Isaiah 53, the suffering servant, four times in five verses.
2.mean: ‘Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you should follow in His footsteps: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth.”’ ‘When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate’, but ‘entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly. He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. “By His stripes you are healed.”’ ‘For “you were like sheep going astray,” but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.’
2.big: Christ is both our example in suffering and our substitute who bore our sins.
2.diff: ‘He Himself bore our sins’. Christians across traditions read this as Christ taking our sins on himself in his death, the heart of the doctrine of substitution. ‘By His stripes you are healed’. In context the healing is from sin, ‘so that we might die to sin’. Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians also see physical healing as provided for in Christ’s death, to be fully received at the resurrection and sometimes now (compare Matthew 8:16–17). Others think that goes beyond Peter’s point here.

3.ctx: A Christian wife with a pagan husband was in a delicate position, in a society where the husband normally decided the religion of the household.
3.mean: ‘Wives, in the same way, submit yourselves to your husbands, so that even if they refuse to believe the word, they will be won over without words by the behavior of their wives’. Real beauty is ‘the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious in God’s sight.’ They are Sarah’s daughters ‘if you do what is right and refuse to give way to fear.’ ‘Husbands, in the same way, treat your wives with consideration as a delicate vessel, and with honor as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life, so that your prayers will not be hindered.’
3.big: A believing spouse’s character can win an unbelieving partner, and husbands must honour their wives as equal heirs of life.
3.diff: Submission in marriage. As at Ephesians 5 and Colossians 3, Christians differ on how this applies today (complementarian and egalitarian readings). Note that Peter tells wives not to ‘give way to fear’: submission is not giving in to intimidation, and never means accepting abuse. ‘A delicate vessel’ (older versions: ‘the weaker vessel’) is usually taken to refer to physical strength and social vulnerability, not spiritual or moral worth; in the same breath Peter calls wives ‘fellow heirs’. And a husband who mistreats his wife damages his own relationship with God.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Peter (trans. Owen), CCEL

3.ctx: Peter sums up with a quotation from Psalm 34:12–16.
3.mean: ‘All of you, be like-minded and sympathetic, love as brothers, be tenderhearted and humble. Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with blessing’. ‘Whoever would love life and see good days must keep his tongue from evil’, ‘turn from evil and do good’, ‘seek peace and pursue it.’
3.big: Christians answer insult with blessing, as their Lord did.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on 1 Peter (trans. Owen), CCEL

3.ctx: Believers might be dragged before local magistrates or questioned by hostile neighbours. Peter prepares them.
3.mean: ‘Even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed.’ ‘But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect’. ‘For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God. He was put to death in the body but made alive in the Spirit, in whom He also went and preached to the spirits in prison who disobeyed long ago… in the days of Noah’. In the ark eight people ‘were saved through water. And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also—not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ’, who now reigns over all powers.
3.big: Christ suffered once for all to bring us to God, and now reigns over every power; so believers can face suffering without fear.
3.diff: ‘A defense’ (Greek apologia) is the word from which ‘apologetics’ comes. It is to be given ‘with gentleness and respect’. The spirits in prison (verses 19–20) are among the hardest verses in the New Testament. Main views: (1) Through the Spirit, Christ preached through Noah to the people of Noah’s day, who are now ‘in prison’. Wesley: ‘Through the ministry of Noah’, to ‘The unholy men before the flood’. (2) Between his death and resurrection Christ went to the realm of the dead. Catholic teaching links this to the creed’s ‘He descended into hell’: ‘Jesus did not descend into hell to deliver the damned, nor to destroy the hell of damnation, but to free the just who had gone before him’ (Catechism 633). Calvin held that the grace of Christ was made known to ‘godly spirits’ who had died, and insisted ‘there is no hope left for those who continue to death unbelieving.’ (3) After his resurrection Christ proclaimed his victory to the fallen angels imprisoned for their rebellion in Noah’s time (compare 2 Peter 2:4–5; Jude 6). Many modern scholars hold this view, noting that ‘spirits’ used on its own like this refers elsewhere in the Bible to supernatural beings, not to people who have died. None of these views teaches a second chance of salvation after death. ‘Baptism that now saves you’. Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran churches read this as showing that baptism is God’s means of salvation (the Catechism: ‘Baptism is necessary for salvation’, 1257). Reformed and Baptist readers stress Peter’s own qualification: ‘not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God’, ‘through the resurrection’. Calvin: ‘baptism in its main part is spiritual.’ Wesley called it ‘The thing typified by the ark’. All agree that it is Christ’s resurrection, not water, that has the power to save.

4.ctx: Former pagan friends found the believers’ changed lives strange, and mocked them.
4.mean: ‘Since Christ suffered in His body, arm yourselves with the same resolve’. Live ‘for the will of God’, not human passions. Former friends ‘consider it strange of you not to plunge with them into the same flood of reckless indiscretion, and they heap abuse on you. But they will have to give an account’. ‘The end of all things is near.’ So pray, ‘love one another deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins’, show hospitality without complaining, and use every gift ‘to serve one another’, ‘so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ’.
4.big: Because the end is near, believers live for God’s will, love deeply and use their gifts to serve one another.
4.diff: ‘The gospel was preached even to those who are now dead’ (verse 6). Most interpreters take this to mean believers who heard the gospel in their lifetime and have since died: men judged them, but they live to God. Catholic teaching connects it with Christ’s descent to the dead (Catechism 634: ‘The gospel was preached even to the dead’). The BSB’s ‘now dead’ reflects the first reading. ‘Love covers over a multitude of sins’ (from Proverbs 10:12) means love forgives and does not keep bringing up wrongs, not that love earns forgiveness from God.

4.ctx: ‘Christian’ was probably first a nickname given by outsiders (Acts 11:26). Peter uses it here, one of only three times in the New Testament. See What kind of persecution? above.
4.mean: ‘Do not be surprised at the fiery trial that has come upon you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ’. ‘If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed’. They must not suffer for wrongdoing, ‘But if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but glorify God that you bear that name.’ ‘So then, those who suffer according to God’s will should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good.’
4.big: Suffering for being a Christian is no surprise and no shame; it is sharing in Christ’s sufferings.

5.ctx: Peter writes as ‘a fellow elder’, not as a ruler over them.
5.mean: ‘As a fellow elder, a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and a partaker of the glory to be revealed, I appeal to the elders among you: Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you, watching over them not out of compulsion, but willingly… not out of greed, but out of eagerness; not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock. And when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the crown of glory that will never fade away.’
5.big: Church leaders are under-shepherds, serving willingly and by example, answerable to the Chief Shepherd.
5.diff: Peter, the leading apostle, calls himself ‘a fellow elder’. Catholic teaching holds that Peter had a unique role among the apostles, continued in the bishop of Rome (Matthew 16:18). Protestants and Orthodox read this verse as showing Peter’s humility and a shared leadership. All can agree on the picture of leadership here: willing, unselfish, and by example.

5.ctx: Peter quotes Proverbs 3:34. He had once denied Jesus out of fear, and had been restored (John 21:15–19).
5.mean: ‘All of you, clothe yourselves with humility toward one another, because, “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” Humble yourselves, therefore, under God’s mighty hand, so that in due time He may exalt you. Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you. Be sober-minded and alert. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, standing firm in your faith’. Believers everywhere are suffering the same things.
5.big: Humble trust in God, who cares for us, is how believers stand against the devil.

5.ctx: The closing words. See ‘Babylon’, Mark, and Peter’s death in Rome above.
5.mean: ‘After you have suffered for a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to His eternal glory in Christ, will Himself restore you, secure you, strengthen you, and establish you.’ ‘Through Silvanus… I have written to you briefly’, ‘testifying that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it.’ ‘The church in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you greetings, as does my son Mark.’
5.big: Suffering is brief; the God of all grace will restore and establish his people.
5.diff: ‘My son Mark’ is spiritual, not physical: Mark had become like a son to Peter. This fits the early tradition that Mark’s Gospel records Peter’s preaching.
